title: Once
full_review:
"Once" (Fox Searchlight) is a gritty, bare-bones story about musicians that is several notches above more sugarcoated fare like "Music and Lyrics."

A winner of the Sundance Film Festival World Cinema Audience Award, "Once" is a low-budget independent film with an unknown cast, though be warned: Many of the Irish accents are thicker than ale. Nonetheless, it has heart in abundance.

The two leads, referred to as Guy (Glen Hansard) and Girl (Marketa Irglova), meet on the streets of Dublin where he is singing and playing a dilapidated guitar for money. He lives with his dad and they repair vacuum cleaners. He still pines over a girlfriend who moved to London. She is a Czech immigrant who lives with her mother, has a baby girl, sells flowers on the street and cleans houses.

Through their shared love of music, they forge a deep connection based on the international language of music, despite the language barrier. Their artistic bond overshadows their meager lifestyles, and through sheer talent and persistence they raise money to create a band, book a recording studio and make a demo tape. The heartfelt Celtic folk-rock music is a highlight of the movie.

The two leads are so harmonious -- in real life, they actually released a joint album -- that the bittersweet resolution is both sad and uplifting. Writer-director John Carney is also a musician, and his love for the craft of creating music shows in every frame.

The film contains alcohol use, a minor street scuffle and recurring rough language and mild profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
